content.rationale: Variance-normalized additive fusion of bottleneck and encoder Mahalanobis distances combines sensitivity to near-OOS held-out intents with sensitivity to far-domain OOS queries.

In-scope encoder representations should lie near a low-dimensional principal subspace learned from training data, while OOS queries often retain larger residual components. Combining this residual with energy captures both representation-level novelty and classifier uncertainty.

Averaging several local neighbor distances in normalized bottleneck space estimates whether a query lies in a supported in-scope neighborhood while reducing sensitivity to an unusually close individual training example.

Trailing within-class covariance directions emphasize low-variance constraints that in-scope representations satisfy but OOS queries often violate. A train-calibrated energy term complements this representation-space signal with classifier uncertainty.

A query confidently assigned to a class can still be OOS if its representation is atypical for that predicted class. Class-wise robust calibration makes predicted-class Mahalanobis distances comparable across intents with different spread.

In-scope predictions tend to have both a clearer top-two class separation and a larger centered-logit magnitude. Combining train-calibrated deficits in these two logit-shape measures flags uncertain, low-concentration OOS outputs.

L2-normalized bottleneck features remove representation magnitude and measure angular agreement with class prototypes. OOS queries should have lower cosine similarity to every in-scope class prototype.

Empirical-CDF calibration puts classifier energy and pooled-feature Mahalanobis novelty on a shared train-derived scale. Summing their upper-tail evidence detects queries that are uncertain in logit space, atypical in representation space, or both.

The normalized Dirichlet concentration shape captures top-two ambiguity independently of total evidence: OOS queries often assign unusually similar concentration to the predicted and runner-up intents. Predicted-class conditional empirical calibration accounts for different in-scope ambiguity levels across intents.

Low-energy confident queries retain the classifier's energy ordering, while high-energy uncertain queries are evaluated primarily by their pooled-feature distance from in-scope classes. This conditional gate uses representation novelty only where logits indicate that the classifier is unreliable.

Class-specific shrunk diagonal variances preserve intent-dependent feature scales that a tied covariance loses. Distance to the classifier-predicted intent then flags queries that are confident but geometrically inconsistent with that intent.

Class-mean directions describe the representation subspace most useful for separating known intents. OOS queries can retain substantial pooled-feature energy orthogonal to this discriminative subspace.

Bottleneck and encoder density deficits are fused with weights learned from train-only pseudo-OOS boundary samples formed between neighboring intent classes. This calibrates each representation level by how strongly it distinguishes supported in-scope examples from cross-intent feature regions.

ViM treats the norm outside the principal in-scope representation subspace as a virtual OOS logit. Queries with substantial residual feature energy receive high virtual-class probability even when an in-scope intent logit is confident.

Moderately large-k cosine neighbor distance in encoder space measures whether a query is supported by a stable local in-scope neighborhood rather than by one accidental close example. Pooled representations retain semantic information that can expose OOS queries despite confident classifier logits.

Low-variance within-class directions encode constraints that in-scope representations tend to satisfy. Combining train-calibrated trailing-direction deviations from bottleneck and pooled spaces captures violations at two semantic levels.

An in-scope query's classifier-predicted intent should also be geometrically close to its nearest Gaussian intent region. Positive disagreement between the predicted-class distance and the nearest-class distance flags queries whose logits and representation support conflict.
OOS queries often have both a reduced top-two logit margin and unusually low centered-logit concentration; class-conditional train calibration accounts for intent-specific logit scales.

A query may be close to some intent prototype yet disagree geometrically with the intent selected by the classifier. Class-conditional calibration of cosine agreement between normalized bottleneck features and the predicted intent prototype flags such logit-representation mismatches.

Energy and bottleneck-space relative Mahalanobis distance capture complementary classifier uncertainty and representation novelty. Train-only ECDF calibration maps both signals to a common upper-tail scale before combining them.

Normalized Dirichlet concentration vectors describe the allocation pattern of evidential support independently of total evidence. OOS inputs can exhibit concentration shapes atypical of the intent selected by the classifier, including confidently misallocated evidence.

A train-calibrated soft gate preserves energy-based ordering for confident items, but progressively substitutes pooled-feature novelty when energy indicates uncertainty. This targets uncertain queries whose representation is either unsupported by, or unusually close to, the in-scope feature distribution.

Class-specific shrunk diagonal Gaussian likelihoods retain intent-dependent feature scales while avoiding unstable full covariance estimates. OOS queries should have low likelihood under every in-scope intent, rather than only under their predicted intent.

Removing the class-mean discriminative subspace isolates feature variation not needed to distinguish known intents. A predicted-intent conditional, shrunk diagonal likelihood in this orthogonal remainder flags inputs with unsupported residual structure.

The norm outside a train-derived principal representation subspace measures unsupported feature content, while energy retains classifier uncertainty information. Train-only robust scaling lets residual novelty contribute without being dominated by feature magnitude.

A query can be globally close to training data while lacking local support from the intent predicted by the classifier. Class-conditional cosine kNN distance measures whether the predicted intent has a semantically similar in-scope neighborhood.

Trailing within-class covariance directions encode low-variance constraints shared by in-scope intent representations. OOS queries that violate these constrained pooled-feature directions receive larger residual scores.

In-scope examples should lie near one intent basin with a clear advantage over competing basins. OOS queries tend to be globally distant from all intent regions or geometrically ambiguous between multiple regions.

The increase in predictive entropy when logits are softened from a sharp to a warm temperature measures spectral temperature-susceptibility beyond MSP or energy. Diffuse OOS logit spectra tend to have a smaller entropy change than supported in-scope predictions.

Energy captures classifier uncertainty while pooled-space neighborhood distance measures local semantic support. Train-only empirical-CDF calibration puts these complementary signals on a common upper-tail scale before combining them.

The entropy of normalized Dirichlet concentrations measures how evidence is allocated across intents, independently of total evidence. Class-conditional deviations from the in-scope allocation sharpness flag evidential shapes atypical for the intent receiving the most support.

Energy is retained unchanged for train-calibrated confident queries, while increasingly uncertain queries are scored by pooled-space Gaussian novelty. This targets OOS inputs whose logits become ambiguous but whose representations remain unsupported by any in-scope intent region.

A predicted intent should assign high likelihood under its own feature-wise variance profile. Class-specific shrunk diagonal covariances preserve intent-dependent feature scales while avoiding unstable covariance estimates.
Projecting out the class-mean discriminative subspace leaves within-intent residual structure, where OOS queries should have weak local support from training examples.

A ViM-style virtual OOS logit converts the norm outside the dominant training-feature subspace into competing evidence against known-class logits. OOS inputs should have larger unsupported residual components and therefore receive more virtual-class probability.

Local Outlier Factor compares each normalized pooled representation's neighborhood density with the densities of its neighbors. OOS queries should have sparse or inconsistent local support even when their nearest in-scope example is moderately close.

Low-variance within-class directions encode constraints that supported intent representations should satisfy. A predicted-class conditional residual score emphasizes violations of these constrained directions while accounting for intent-specific feature centers.

A query may receive a confident logit prediction while its normalized pooled representation is unusually far from that predicted intent's prototype. Class-specific train-calibrated cosine residuals expose this logit-feature disagreement without selecting the nearest class.
The top-two logit margin measures decisiveness among the most plausible intents, while train-calibrated logit norm discounts uniformly weak but accidentally separated predictions.

MSP uncertainty and pooled-space Mahalanobis distance capture complementary failures: unsupported queries can be uncertain, geometrically distant, or both. Train empirical-CDF calibration places both signals on a shared in-distribution tail scale before fusion.

The centered log-ratio shape of Dirichlet concentrations captures how evidential mass is distributed across intents, independent of total concentration or vacuity. Queries whose evidential allocation is atypical for their predicted intent receive a larger class-conditional shape distance.

A full but shrinkage-regularized covariance for each intent models intent-specific correlation structure rather than assuming one shared Gaussian shape. Queries confidently routed to an intent but violating that intent's correlated pooled-feature geometry receive large conditional residuals.

The class-mean subspace captures directions that discriminate known intents, while the orthogonal complement measures semantic variation unsupported by those intent directions. OOS inputs should have unusually large and disproportionately off-subspace residual energy.

The residual norm outside a global in-scope principal subspace measures encoder variation unsupported by training representations, while energy captures classifier uncertainty. Train-calibrated tail scores combine geometric novelty with uncertain intent assignment.
OOS queries tend to require a larger expansion from their nearest semantic neighbor to a broader local neighborhood, reflecting weak or fragmented in-scope support.

Trailing within-class covariance directions encode constraints that supported intents satisfy. Normalizing trailing-direction residual energy by total partial-spectrum energy emphasizes disproportionate violations rather than overall feature magnitude.

In-scope representations should usually have a clearly preferred class prototype, whereas OOS queries often lie between several known intent regions and have a small nearest-versus-second-nearest distance gap.
Known intents tend to produce logits concentrated along one centered class direction, whereas OOS inputs often have a more diffuse centered logit shape even after removing global logit shifts.

L2-normalized pooled representations of in-scope queries should align with their class prototype. Low maximum cosine similarity indicates that a query has weak directional support from every known intent.

Train-calibrated upper-tail probabilities put classifier energy and pooled-space Mahalanobis novelty on a common scale. Their probabilistic union flags queries that are either uncertain in logit space or geometrically unsupported.

The normalized Dirichlet concentration vector describes how evidence is allocated across intents independently of total evidence. OOS queries can have an atypical evidential allocation relative to the in-scope intent selected by the classifier, producing a large Jensen-Shannon divergence.

Energy remains the primary score for confident predictions, while a train-calibrated Mahalanobis residual is activated mainly in the uncertain energy tail. This emphasizes feature-space novelty when classifier uncertainty alone is ambiguous.
Different intents can occupy differently dispersed regions of representation space, so a shrinkage diagonal Gaussian mixture assigns low density to queries unsupported by every intent.
Directions that linearly explain class-logit variation are the classifier's discriminative feature subspace; OOS queries should retain unusually large energy in its orthogonal remainder.

A ViM-style residual norm measures encoder-feature energy outside the principal in-scope subspace. Queries with semantic variation unsupported by the training representation manifold should have larger residuals.

A query should be locally supported both in the encoder's semantic pooled space and in the classifier bottleneck space. Combining train-normalized neighborhood radii across these complementary representations highlights examples that lack support in either geometry.

Low-variance within-class directions encode constraints that supported intents tend to satisfy. A class-conditioned, ridge-whitened residual in these trailing directions flags inputs that violate those constraints.

A query confidently predicted as a known intent should lie near that predicted intent's representation prototype. Class-specific radial normalization makes distances comparable across intents with different semantic spread.

The top-two centered-logit margin measures whether one intent is decisively preferred over its closest competitor, independently of shared logit shifts captured by energy. OOS queries often have unusually small margins despite potentially moderate overall logit scale.

Classifier entropy and pooled-space Mahalanobis novelty capture complementary OOS signals. Mapping each to its train empirical tail probability makes their consensus directly comparable without using eval-set statistics.

The normalized Dirichlet concentration shape describes how evidential mass is allocated among intents independently of total evidence. OOS examples should have an allocation pattern poorly supported by every class-conditional in-scope evidential shape model.
Energy remains the score for clearly in-scope-looking items, while a train-calibrated semantic neighborhood radius is smoothly emphasized only in the uncertain energy tail.
Intent representations can have substantially different per-coordinate dispersion, so a regularized class-specific diagonal Gaussian assigns low support to queries unlike every intent.

The fraction of feature energy outside a train-derived principal semantic subspace measures manifold violation while being less sensitive to overall feature norm. Combining its train-standardized value with energy captures both unsupported semantic variation and classifier uncertainty.

Averaging several local neighbor distances in L2-normalized pooled space estimates semantic support more stably than a single-neighbor radius. OOS queries should have consistently weak support across a moderate local neighborhood.

Within-class trailing covariance directions encode constraints that supported intents tend to satisfy. The ratio of trailing to leading residual energy highlights violations while reducing sensitivity to overall representation magnitude.

After removing the per-item shared logit shift, in-scope examples tend to have a class-discriminative logit-shape norm supported by training data. Low centered-logit norm flags diffuse intent allocation independently of energy.

Classifier energy and pooled-space Mahalanobis novelty are calibrated separately within the classifier's predicted intent, so naturally difficult intents do not dominate either signal. Averaging their train-calibrated Gaussian quantiles flags queries that are unusually uncertain or geometrically unsupported for the intent they resemble.
